docs.title: Andrea Vitaletti
docs.text:
Andrea Vitaletti, Ph.D., Associate Professor of Computer Science at Sapienza University of Rome. My research focuses on designing systems for collecting, analyzing, and managing data in distributed networks, with a strong emphasis on decentralized governance. Over the years, I have worked on the Internet of Things (IoT), Distributed Ledger Technologies (DLT), and Federated Machine Learning, topics I also teach at Sapienza. More recently, my research has focused on Verifiable Computation and Computational Gastronomy.

I am particularly interested in the trade-offs between data utility and privacy, as well as the balance between individual and collective interests in digital ecosystems. I have co-authored over 90 scientific papers and contributed to several European research projects, including serving as principal investigator and coordinator of the FET Open project PLEASED.

A maker at heart, I have hands-on experience in technology transfer. I co-founded the spin-offs WLAB (exit in 2016) and WSENSE (which I left in 2019). Since 2020, I have been teaching Digital Entrepreneurship, and I’m proud to see some of my students launch their own startups, such as iotilize.me and yeastime.

Hobbies: Traveling, sailing, cycling, and paragliding. I also play the piano and guitar for fun... you’ve been warned!

docs.title: Grains of Insight: A Data Science Perspective on Rice in Gastronomy
docs.text:
Rice is a foundational ingredient in global gastronomy, but its culinary significance varies greatly across cultures. This project, funded by MAECI, explores the role of rice through a data science lens, with a particular focus on two gastronomically rich contexts: Korea and Italy. While Korea embraces rice as a daily staple central to dishes like bap, bibimbap, and tteok, Italy incorporates rice in regionally distinctive ways—most notably in risotto, arancini, and traditional desserts—highlighting its versatility beyond mere sustenance.

By analyzing large-scale datasets from recipe repositories, food blogs, culinary texts, and nutritional sources, the research will uncover how rice is embedded in the culinary identity of each country. Techniques from natural language processing (NLP), machine learning, and statistical analysis will be used to map usage patterns, cooking methods, ingredient pairings, and regional trends.

The project will also consider historical, cultural, and socioeconomic factors influencing rice consumption and transformation in both nations. By contrasting these two case studies, the research will offer insights into how a common ingredient can serve vastly different gastronomic roles shaped by culture.

The findings will benefit culinary historians, chefs, and food system researchers, while promoting interdisciplinary dialogue between data science and gastronomy. Ultimately, the project aims to show how rice, though humble in form, carries deep cultural meaning and culinary innovation.

This project is also a unique opportunity to strengthen the already on-going collaboration between the Korean and Italian research groups that are currently organizing together the 1st International Workshop on on Computational Gastronomy: Data Science for Food and Cooking.

docs.title: Blockchain fork & proof-of-work demo
docs.text:
A small, dependency-free blockchain that runs entirely in the browser. Each browser tab is an independent node: nodes talk to each other over the BroadcastChannel API (same-origin cross-tab messaging), mine blocks with a real (tiny) proof-of-work, and resolve competing chains with the longest-chain rule.

code

docs.title: Try it with multiple nodes
docs.text:
BroadcastChannel is scoped to the whole site origin, not to this one embedded frame, so you can get several independent nodes talking to each other either way:

  • open this page in two or more browser tabs, or
  • open the demo directly, outside the frame, at code/blockchain-demo/index.html, in two or more tabs.

Mining a block in one tab should show up in the others after a short simulated network delay — watch the "Network log" section.

docs.title: What it demonstrates
docs.text:
• Async hashing — block hashes are computed with the browser's native crypto.subtle.digest (Web Crypto), which is asynchronous.
  • Simulated network latency — incoming messages are delivered after a random delay, so tabs behave like nodes talking over a slow/unreliable network rather than making instantaneous local calls.
  • Proof of work — mining repeatedly re-hashes a block with an incrementing nonce until the hash has enough leading zero hex digits. "Mine block" is disabled while this runs and reports how long it took.
  • Forks and the longest-chain rule — if two nodes mine a block on the same tip before hearing about each other, both reject each other's block and diverge. Whichever branch is extended further eventually wins: once a node hears about a chain longer than its own (and valid), it discards its own chain and adopts that one.

All of these knobs (simulated network delay, proof-of-work difficulty) live in one place in the demo's config.js, so they're easy to tune to make forks easier or harder to trigger.

docs.title: Trigger a fork on purpose
docs.text:
1. Open three tabs of the demo. Confirm all three show the same single genesis entry in "Chain".
  2. In two of the tabs, type some data and click "Mine block" in both as close together as possible.
  3. Wait for the simulated network delay to settle, then check each tab's chain: the two that mined will have kept their own block, and the third will have adopted whichever arrived first — a fork.
  4. Keep mining in one of the forked tabs (or the third one) until its chain is longer than the other branch. Watch the losing tab's log: once a longer, valid chain arrives, it logs a "chain replaced (longest-chain rule)" message and adopts it. Give it another round of network delay and all tabs converge on the same chain.

Data-Driven vs. Data-Informed Design
docs.text:
Data is nowadays the universal currency. This is true also for design, however, how designers choose to spend that currency defines the final product. The terms data-driven and data-informed are often used interchangeably, but they represent fundamentally different philosophical approaches to innovation.

This distinction determines whether data is the master of the design process, or a highly valued consultant.

docs.title: Defining the Approaches
docs.text:
• Data-Driven Design: The data dictates the decision. This is an objective, often algorithmic approach where specific, high-confidence data points automate or directly generate the design outcome. (e.g., "If \(X\) increases by \(10\%\), then design must change by \(Y\%\).")
  • Data-Informed Design: Data is an input, not the answer. This is a holistic approach that interprets data alongside other critical, often subjective factors: human intuition, empathy, context, user feedback, and brand identity. Data informs the designer's judgment, but the final decision rests on human understanding.

docs.title: The Evolution of a Running Shoe: From Intuition to Algorithm
docs.text:
To illustrate these concepts, we can simulate the evolution of a professional marathon running shoe. A shoe is a good candidate for this comparison because its function is strictly measurable by performance data (seconds, energy cost), yet its adoption depends entirely on subjective experience (comfort, perception).

This journey, visualized below, moves from a simple starting point (intuition), through an impactful (but blunt) use of data, to the highly sophisticated engineering loop that drives a "Super Shoe."

docs.title: Stage 1: The Intuitive Baseline
docs.text:
We begin with a traditional shoe: "Generation 1: The Baseline (Intuition Model)."

Here, data is almost entirely absent. The design is based on intuition and basic, static data, such as average foot size (anthropometrics). This model represents the "way we've always done it."

The Consequence: While simple and functional, this shoe fails to address dynamic forces. A force plate study of a runner in this shoe would show high, unmanaged peaks of impact force at the heel (the red spike in an imaginary graph). It is intuitive for basic walking, but not mathematically optimized for running 26.2 miles.

docs.title: Stage 2: Data-Driven Impact Management
docs.text:
In "Generation 2: Impact-Driven," the design moves to a true data-driven loop.

The Data Input: The design team acquires dynamic Force Plate data from thousands of runners. This objective data reveals the precise magnitude and location of impact during a full marathon gait cycle.

The Data-Driven Choice: The data mandates a change. The designers do not sketch a wedge; an algorithm calculates the exact required volume and taper of EVA foam midsole needed to attenuate that specific force and prevent it from "bottoming out" against the asphalt.

The Clear Outcome: This objective change yields an objective metric: a measured 20% reduction in knee strain.

docs.title: Stage 3: Data-Informed Efficiency Optimization (The "Super Shoe")
docs.text:
This final stage, "Generation 3: The Super Shoe," is where the concepts of data-driven and data-informed truly diverge.

This shoe must optimize running economy (the metabolic cost of moving), which is a complex function of mechanical advantage (data-driven) and subjective comfort (data-informed).

Design Element A Purely DATA-DRIVEN Approach A DATA-INFORMED Approach Midsole Plate Curve The optimal curved shape of the carbon fiber plate is generated via 3D Finite Element Analysis (FEA), simulating maximum energy return at \(40\text{mm}\) of midsole thickness. The plate is included, but its aggressive curvature is modified. Professional athletes test the \(40\text{mm}\) version and report feeling "wobbly" or unstable. The designer chooses to use the high-efficiency foam but reduces the midsole height to \(38\text{mm}\) to increase perceived security and decrease ankle roll risk, accepting a negligible loss in theoretical energy return for a major gain in practical confidence. Lacing System The system is generated by an algorithmic pattern that evenly distributes tensile stress based on pressure maps (objective pressure). A designer reviews the data but overlays subjective feedback. The algorithm's pattern requires \(14\) lace eyelets, which runners find tedious to use and "too fussy" for a high-stress race environment. The system is redesigned to use only \(6\) ergonomic eyelets that "feel" more intuitive and secure.

The "Super Shoe" of Generation 3 is only possible because both disciplines are applied. The carbon plate and Pebax foam are data-driven interventions based on VO2 sensors and energy transfer calculations. But their final shape, placement, and ergonomic integration, the elements that make a shoe feel fast, are data-informed decisions made by a designer who trusts the numbers, but prioritizes the athlete.

docs.title: Approach and proxies
docs.text:
In principle, the data-informed approach permeates every phase of Design Thinking, providing the empirical scaffolding for creative decisions. However, a significant challenge arises: the most critical design 'pinpoints', particularly those involving qualitative human experience, often elude direct sensing.

When sensors cannot capture the nuance of a 'feeling,' the designer’s role shifts. It becomes a fundamental task of the designer to bridge this gap by designing a proxy: a method of translating inherently qualitative, subjective experiences into measurable, actionable data points. In this context, the designer doesn't just use data; they design the instruments that bring the 'unmeasurable' into the light.

In the evolution of our Generation 3 Super Shoe, a major qualitative hurdle is Stability.

The Qualitative Problem: Runners report that while the new carbon-plate shoes are fast, they feel "nervous" or "unstable" during sharp turns or on uneven pavement. There is no "Confidence Sensor" to plug into a runner's brain to measure this anxiety.

The Data-Driven Failure: A standard sensor might measure Ankle Pronation Angle. The data shows the ankle is only moving \(2^\circ\) more than usual—statistically negligible. A data-driven approach might ignore the runners' complaints because the "numbers look fine."

The Designer’s Proxy (The Solution):

The designer needs a proxy for "Confidence." They decide to measure "Step Frequency Variability during Directional Change."

  1. The Logic: When a human feels stable and confident, their gait is rhythmic and consistent. When they feel "nervous" about their footing, their brain makes micro-adjustments, causing tiny, irregular fluctuations in the timing between steps (cadence jitter).
  2. The Measurement: By using high-frequency accelerometers, the designer measures the Standard Deviation of Step Time (\(ms\)) during a \(90^\circ\) turn.
  3. The Result: The proxy works. The data shows that in Shoe A, the cadence is erratic during turns, while in Shoe B, it remains steady.

By designing this proxy, the designer has turned a "vague feeling of nervousness" into a hard numerical value that can be used to iterate the design of the shoe's outsole flare or traction pattern.

docs.title: Comparison of Direct vs. Proxy Measurement
docs.text:
Qualitative Goal Direct Sensor (Impossible) Designer’s Proxy (The "Hack") User Comfort "Pleasure" probe in the brain. Micro-shift Frequency: Measuring how often a user shifts their weight or adjusts the shoe laces over a \(2\)-hour period. Product Premiumness "Luxury" meter. Decibel/Frequency Analysis: The specific "thud" or "click" sound the shoe makes on pavement (Lower frequencies are often perceived as "sturdier" and more premium). Mental Fatigue Direct neuron monitoring. Pupil Dilation / Eye-Track Jitter: Measuring how much visual focus is required to maintain balance on a treadmill.

How I wrote this document

I sketch the concept roughly, Gemini (in this case) provides a cleaner version, I review the version and iterate up to a point where I'm satisfied. It is a fair example of a collaborative, data-informed feedback loop ;-)

docs.title: IoT for Product Design
docs.text:
📊 Course Slides: Download Presentation Slides (PDF) | View Slide Source (Marp Markdown)

Course Agreement & Ground Rules

  • Use of AI is perfectly fine, but it is not an excuse to do not understand
  • At the end I want to see a physical product made of real interconnected things
  • No validation is unacceptable and dangerous
  • Validation needs measures, not generic sentences

docs.title: 1. Purpose
docs.text:
This set of exercises introduces product design students to the Internet of Things (IoT) through hands-on work with ESP32 boards programmed in Arduino. It has two goals:

  1. From smart objects to ecosystems. Show that sensors, actuators and connectivity let us build an ecosystem of cooperating objects, not just isolated smart objects. The value comes from the relationships between objects, people and services.
  2. From data to better products. Show that the data IoT devices collect can improve the design, development, use and maintenance of a product or service, closing the loop between the designer and the product in the field.

The path goes step by step. Each exercise introduces one or two new concepts and reuses the skills from the previous ones. Every exercise ends with a short design reflection, because the aim is to train designers who understand what the technology makes possible, not to train embedded engineers.

The connected parts of the course are built on an open standard, MQTT, rather than on a proprietary platform. The class is made of designers with little experience of programming tools, so the priority is to keep the number of tools, accounts and concepts as low as possible. Four tools are used, each with a clear role:

Tool What it is for Limits Wokwi (browser simulator) Sketching and trying behaviour, with no hardware and no risk — including Wi-Fi and MQTT Limited number of simulations on the Free plan Arduino IDE 2 (desktop app) Uploading to the real board, Serial Monitor/Plotter, unlimited uploads Does not create dashboards MQTTX (desktop / web app) Looking inside the network: watching every message of the studio, sending commands by hand A debugging tool, not an interface for end users ThingsBoard (demo server) Only when necessary: dashboards for other people, history, alarms, remote settings, fleet management Shared public demo server: not for personal or sensitive data

Objects talk to each other through a public MQTT broker (e.g. test.mosquitto.org): no account, no quota, and it works both from the real board and from Wokwi. ThingsBoard enters the course from Exercise 6, when the object must be used, monitored and configured by people who are not its programmers.

Setup notes. On Linux install pyserial for the upload tool: sudo apt update && sudo apt install python3-serial. In the Arduino IDE install the esp32 board package (by Espressif) and the PubSubClient library (by Nick O'Leary).

If necessary reduce the upload speed

Going deeper: the IoT course

Many topics of this course are treated in more technical depth in the IoT course notes. Where useful, exercises below have a Reference line pointing to the relevant page, e.g. Simulating a node, A real node, MQTT and ThingsBoard.

docs.title: 2. Running scenario: "The Connected Studio"
docs.text:
To keep the exercises coherent, they all share one scenario: a shared studio / co-working room that the class progressively "brings to life".

  • Every group designs and builds one object for the studio, e.g. a desk lamp, a "focus" totem, a plant pot, a window/air-quality monitor, a doorbell/presence badge, a coffee corner counter, or a noise meter. All objects are described in the Studio Object Catalogue.
  • In the first exercises each object works alone (smart object).
  • Later the objects talk to each other through shared MQTT topics (ecosystem).
  • Finally the objects are used for real for sometimes, and the data they produce is used to redesign them (data-driven design).

This scenario makes both goals concrete. Students experience first-hand what changes when their object is no longer alone, and when it starts "reporting back" how it is actually used.

docs.title: 3. Target audience and prerequisites
docs.text:
• Product design students (bachelor or master level) with limited experience of digital tools for programming.
  • No prior programming experience is required. Variables, if and loops are introduced in Exercises 0–1, always starting from working examples that students modify rather than write from scratch.
  • Groups of 2–3 students, one hardware kit per group.
  • Each student needs a laptop with a Chromium-based browser or Firefox, the Arduino IDE 2 (with the ESP32 package and the PubSubClient library) and MQTTX. From Exercise 6 each group needs a (free) account on demo.thingsboard.io. A smartphone with an MQTT dashboard app (e.g. IoT MQTT Panel, or the MQTTX web client in the browser) is useful from Exercise 5.

docs.title: 4. Hardware kit (per group)
docs.text: The kit is split into two parts: a Core Kit containing the bare minimal interaction primitives (the 4 digital and continuous inputs/outputs) used by everyone from day one without any external libraries, and Specialized Project Modules introduced from Exercise 3 according to each group's studio object.

docs.title: 4.1 Core Kit (Universal — used from Exercise 0)
docs.text:
These components require zero external libraries and form the foundational 2×2 matrix of physical computing interaction:

Discrete / Binary (0 or 1) Continuous / Modulated (0 … Max) Input (Controls & Sensors) Push Button (digitalRead, INPUT_PULLUP) Potentiometer (analogRead, 0–4095) Output (Feedback & Actuators) LED On/Off (digitalWrite, HIGH/LOW) LED Dimmer (analogWrite, PWM 0–255)

This 2×2 foundation covers the universal vocabulary of physical product interfaces (switches, indicators, knobs, and dimmers) and maps 1-to-1 to the digital controls used later on phone panels and ThingsBoard dashboards:

Interaction Primitive Physical Component Arduino Function Digital counterpart (Phase B) Digital Output Standard LED digitalWrite() LED / status indicator Digital Input Push Button digitalRead() Button / switch (publishes a command) Analog Input Rotary Potentiometer analogRead() Gauge / chart PWM Output LED Dimmer analogWrite() Slider (publishes a value)

docs.title: Core Kit Components:
docs.text:
Component Interaction primitive First used in ESP32 DevKit (e.g. ESP32-WROOM-32 or ESP32-S3) Microcontroller with Wi-Fi & Bluetooth Ex 0 Breadboard, jumper wires, USB data cable Prototyping infrastructure Ex 0 Standard LEDs (red, green, blue) + 220–330 Ω resistors Digital Output (digitalWrite) & PWM Output (analogWrite) Ex 0 / Ex 2 Push buttons Digital Input (digitalRead with internal INPUT_PULLUP) Ex 1 Rotary potentiometer (10 kΩ) Analog Input (analogRead, 0–4095) Ex 2

More on the board and on wiring: Reference hardware · Understanding the breadboard.

docs.title: 4.2 Specialized Project Modules (Introduced from Exercise 3)
docs.text:
Depending on the specific studio object each group designs (desk lamp, presence totem, air quality monitor, plant pot, etc.), groups select from these modules:

Component Purpose & Target Object First used in Light sensor (LDR with 10 kΩ resistor or BH1750 I2C) Ambient light sensing (smart lamp) Ex 3 Temperature/humidity sensor (DHT22 or BME280) Climate & comfort monitoring (air/plant monitor) Ex 3 PIR motion sensor Presence & arrival detection (door badge, focus totem) Ex 3 RGB LED ring (WS2812 / NeoPixel) Expressive multi-color visual output Ex 3 Servo motor (SG90 / micro-servo) Physical motion, indicators, mechanical flags Ex 3 Piezo buzzer Acoustic feedback and alerts Ex 3 Relay module (low voltage only) Switching external appliances / lights Ex 7 (optional) Accelerometer (MPU6050, optional) Handling, vibration, wear monitoring Ex 13 LiPo battery + charger (powering the ESP32, optional) Autonomy, portable power monitoring Ex 13

All components above are available in Wokwi, so every circuit can be simulated before it is wired on the breadboard.

CO₂ and noise are simulated. The kit has no CO₂ sensor (DHT22/BME280 do not measure CO₂) and no microphone. The co2 and noiseLevel values are therefore produced by turning the Core Kit potentiometer, which lets students stage repeatable scenarios, also in Wokwi. See Simulating CO₂ and noise with a potentiometer.

docs.title: 5.1 MQTT first, ThingsBoard when necessary
docs.text:
The backbone of the course is MQTT, the publish/subscribe protocol used by most IoT products. Its mental model fits in one sentence:

The broker is a post office with labelled mailboxes (topics). An object publishes a message to a topic; every object that has subscribed to that topic receives a copy. Publishers and subscribers never need to know each other.

A short introduction to topics and wildcards, with a ready-made Wokwi example, is in Simulating a node → MQTT.

On top of this, ThingsBoard is used only for what plain MQTT does not give: interfaces for people who are not the designers, memory, and fleet management.

Need How it is done Tool Putting the object on the network Wi-Fi + an MQTT client (PubSubClient) connected to a public broker IDE / Wokwi Describing what the object senses and does Topics and payloads (the topic contract, §5.2) MQTT Watching and debugging the network Subscribing to iotpd/studio/# and seeing every message live MQTTX Phone as a remote An MQTT panel app (buttons, sliders, gauges bound to topics) IoT MQTT Panel / MQTTX web Objects talking to objects Shared topics: one object publishes, any other subscribes MQTT Remembering the last state Retained messages: the broker keeps the last value and gives it to whoever subscribes later MQTT Knowing who is online Last Will and Testament (LWT): the broker announces "offline" on behalf of an object that disappears MQTT Dashboards for end users and space owners Dashboards and widgets (value, gauge, chart, switch, slider, LED, image map…), shareable as public links ThingsBoard Places and groups of objects Assets (Studio → Areas) and relations to devices ThingsBoard History and data export Time series stored for each device, chart widgets with time windows, export to CSV/XLS ThingsBoard Alerts Alarm rules in the device profile (with severities), device inactivity detection, notifications ThingsBoard Remote configuration Shared attributes: settings changed from a dashboard and pushed to the object (also on reconnect) ThingsBoard Updating the product in the field OTA firmware update (ArduinoOTA on the local network, or ThingsBoard OTA updates) IDE / ThingsBoard

Two connections, two roles. From Exercise 6 an object may keep two MQTT connections at the same time: one to the studio broker (talking to other objects) and one to ThingsBoard (demo.thingsboard.io, port 1883, authenticated with the device's access token, topic v1/devices/me/telemetry). The first is the object's "conversation with its peers"; the second is its "report to the people who care for it". Keeping them separate is a design choice worth discussing (§8). The ThingsBoard side is explained step by step, with complete sketches, in Backend.

Public servers. test.mosquitto.org and demo.thingsboard.io are free public services for testing: anyone can read (and write!) the topics of a public broker, and the demo server can be reset or slowed down. This is fine — and instructive — for a class prototype, but never for personal data or real products. If the public broker is unreliable, alternatives are broker.hivemq.com and broker.emqx.io, or a Mosquitto broker run by the instructor on the lab network.

docs.title: 5.2 Shared conventions: the "topic contract"
docs.text:
An ecosystem only works if objects "speak the same language". In MQTT this language is made of topic names and payload formats. From Exercise 7 onward the class therefore uses a shared topic contract, defined by the instructor together with the students.

All topics start with a common class prefix, here iotpd/studio (on a public broker, choose a prefix that nobody else is likely to use, e.g. adding the year and university). Values that describe the whole studio live directly under the prefix; values that belong to one object live under its name:

Topic (after iotpd/studio/) Payload Retained Meaning Who publishes studioScene normal | focus | presentation | closed yes Current scene of the studio Scene panel, hub someoneAtDoor 1 (event) no A person has just arrived Door badge roomOccupied 0 | 1 yes Someone is in the room Presence objects co2 integer, ppm yes Air quality Air monitor noiseLevel integer, 0–100 yes Loudness Noise meter <object>/status online | offline yes Set by the object, and by the broker (LWT) Every object <object>/heartbeat integer counter no "I am alive" signal, increases every minute Every object <object>/mode short camelCase word, e.g. focus, inUse yes Current mode of each object Object <object>/set/<name> depends on <name> no A command to the object Panels, hub, others

Each group also documents, for its own object, a product sheet of its topics: topic, payload format, unit, range, retained or not, how often it is published, and what it means for the user.

Rules:

  • Topic levels in camelCase, English, no spaces or accents; units are written in the documentation, not in the topic.
  • Payloads are plain text (812, 1, focus), easy to read in MQTTX and to send from a phone. JSON is used only towards ThingsBoard.
  • State topics (what is) are published by the object itself, usually retained. Command topics (.../set/..., what someone wants) are published by others and never retained. The object obeys a command and then publishes its new state.

Designing this contract is itself a design activity: it is the object's "interface" towards other objects, just as its form and controls are its interface towards people.

docs.title: 5.3 Where to do what
docs.text:
Wokwi can simulate Wi-Fi (network Wokwi-GUEST, no password) and reach public MQTT brokers, so even connected behaviour can be designed without hardware. The rule of thumb given to students:

Step Tool Question it answers 1. Sketch & simulate Wokwi + MQTTX Does the logic work? Do the right messages go out? 2. Try on the real board Arduino IDE 2 + MQTTX Does it work with real sensors, parts and Wi-Fi? 3. Serve people ThingsBoard Does it work as a service for someone who is not me?

Practical tips:

  • MQTTX is the stand-in for any other object. Before your partner's object exists, publish its messages by hand from MQTTX (e.g. iotpd/studio/co2 → 1500) and check how your object reacts.
  • Keep the behaviour in functions. The same functions (e.g. updateLamp(), readSensors()) are reused unchanged from Exercise 3 onward; only the "glue" with MQTT is new.
  • Keep secrets in one file. Wi-Fi password and ThingsBoard access token go in a secrets.h tab, never in screenshots or shared Wokwi projects (see Identity and secret management).
  • Moving from Wokwi to the board is described in From Wokwi to a real device.
  • Use a unique client ID for every connection (e.g. built from the board's MAC address): two clients with the same ID keep kicking each other off the broker.
  • The table in §6 shows, for every exercise, which tools are used.

docs.title: 6. Overview of the path
docs.text:
The exercises are grouped in four phases. The first two phases build the skills; phases C and D address the two main goals directly.

Phase Exercises Key question Goal addressed A — The smart object 0 – 3 What can an object sense, decide and do on its own? Baseline B — The connected object 4 – 6 What changes when an object is on the network? Enabler for 1 & 2 C — The ecosystem 7 – 10 What emerges when objects cooperate? Goal 1 D — Data-driven design 11 – 14 How can data from the field improve the product/service? Goal 2 Final project 15 Design a connected product-service and iterate on it with data 1 + 2
